```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(readxl)
  library(fixest)
  library(ggrepel)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: download
#| include: false
# Census Bureau files, downloaded once into data/acs/. The PUMS file is the
# 2024 American Community Survey 1-year sample, about 1% of the population
# (600 MB zipped).
census <- "https://www2.census.gov"
files <- c(
  csv_pus_2024.zip = "programs-surveys/acs/data/pums/2024/1-Year/csv_pus.zip",
  PUMS_Data_Dictionary_2024.csv =
    "programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/pums/data_dict/PUMS_Data_Dictionary_2024.csv",
  tract_puma_2020.txt = "geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/2020_Census_Tract_to_2020_PUMA.txt",
  cbsa_delineation_2020.xls =
    "programs-surveys/metro-micro/geographies/reference-files/2020/delineation-files/list1_2020.xls"
)
dir.create("data/acs", showWarnings = FALSE)
options(timeout = 3600)
for (f in names(files)) {
  dest <- file.path("data/acs", f)
  if (!file.exists(dest)) download.file(file.path(census, files[[f]]), dest, mode = "wb")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: data
#| include: false
# Person records: the zip holds two CSV files with 3.4 million people.
# Only the columns used here are read.
read_pums <- function(file) {
  path <- unzip("data/acs/csv_pus_2024.zip", files = file, exdir = tempdir())
  on.exit(unlink(path))
  read_csv(path,
           col_select = c(STATE, PUMA, PWGTP, AGEP, SEX, COW, ESR, OCCP,
                          WAGP, WKHP, WKWN, ADJINC),
           col_types = cols(STATE = "c", PUMA = "c", OCCP = "c", .default = "d"))
}
persons <- bind_rows(read_pums("psam_pusa.csv"), read_pums("psam_pusb.csv"))

# Metro areas. The 2020 delineation uses the same counties as the 2020 tract
# file. A PUMA belongs to a metro only if all its tracts are in that metro;
# n_distinct() counts NA (outside any metro) as a value, so PUMAs that cross
# a metro boundary are dropped.
metro_counties <- read_excel("data/acs/cbsa_delineation_2020.xls", skip = 2) |>
  filter(`Metropolitan/Micropolitan Statistical Area` == "Metropolitan Statistical Area") |>
  transmute(county = paste0(`FIPS State Code`, `FIPS County Code`),
            cbsa = `CBSA Code`)
puma_metro <- read_csv("data/acs/tract_puma_2020.txt",
                       col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  transmute(STATE = STATEFP, PUMA = PUMA5CE,
            county = paste0(STATEFP, COUNTYFP)) |>
  left_join(metro_counties, by = "county") |>
  summarise(metros = n_distinct(cbsa), cbsa = first(cbsa), .by = c(STATE, PUMA)) |>
  filter(metros == 1, !is.na(cbsa))

# Metro population: the weighted count of everyone in its PUMAs
metro_pop <- persons |>
  inner_join(puma_metro, by = c("STATE", "PUMA")) |>
  summarise(pop = sum(PWGTP), .by = cbsa)

# Occupation names. Dictionary rows have different numbers of fields, so the
# occupation rows are read on their own.
occupations <- read_lines("data/acs/PUMS_Data_Dictionary_2024.csv") |>
  str_subset("^VAL,OCCP,") |>
  I() |>
  read_csv(col_names = c("type", "variable", "format", "length", "OCCP", "to",
                         "occupation"),
           col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  transmute(OCCP, occupation = str_remove(occupation, "^[A-Z]{3}-"))

# Full-time, full-year wage earners aged 25-64 living in a metro: healthcare
# (codes 3000-3655, without the three veterinary occupations) and lawyers (2100)
healthcare <- setdiff(as.character(c(3000:3550, 3601:3655)), c("3250", "3424", "3648"))
workers <- persons |>
  filter(OCCP %in% c(healthcare, "2100"),
         ESR %in% 1:2, COW %in% 1:5,  # employed, working for wages
         between(AGEP, 25, 64), WKHP >= 35, WKWN >= 50, WAGP > 0) |>
  inner_join(puma_metro, by = c("STATE", "PUMA")) |>
  left_join(metro_pop, by = "cbsa") |>
  left_join(occupations, by = "OCCP") |>
  mutate(wage = WAGP * ADJINC / 1e6, female = SEX == 2)

# Skill = the occupation's average wage. Occupations with fewer than 200
# workers in the sample are dropped.
skill <- workers |>
  filter(OCCP %in% healthcare) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_wage = weighted.mean(wage, PWGTP),
            .by = c(OCCP, occupation)) |>
  filter(n >= 200)

# Top earners: occupations averaging $200,000 or more
top_cutoff <- 200000
health <- workers |>
  inner_join(select(skill, OCCP, mean_wage), by = "OCCP") |>
  mutate(top = mean_wage >= top_cutoff)
```

```{r}
#| label: models
#| include: false
# Pay difference between a metro of 5 million and one of 250,000, in percent,
# from an elasticity of pay with respect to metro population
big_vs_small <- function(b) 100 * (exp(b * log(5e6 / 250000)) - 1)

# Urban wage premium of each occupation: log wage on log metro population,
# holding age and sex fixed. Standard errors clustered by metro.
estimates <- function(models) {
  coeftable(models, keep = "pop") |>
    transmute(OCCP = as.character(sample), b = Estimate, se = `Std. Error`)
}
premium_by_occupation <- function(data) {
  feols(log(wage) ~ log(pop) + AGEP + I(AGEP^2) + female,
        data = data, weights = ~PWGTP, split = ~OCCP, cluster = ~cbsa) |>
    estimates()
}

# Concentration: Poisson regression of a group's weighted worker count in
# every metro, zeros included, on log population. 1 = spread like
# population; above 1 = concentrated in big metros.
concentration_by <- function(group) {
  health |>
    count(cbsa, group = {{ group }}, wt = PWGTP, name = "workers") |>
    complete(cbsa = metro_pop$cbsa, group, fill = list(workers = 0)) |>
    left_join(metro_pop, by = "cbsa") |>
    fepois(workers ~ log(pop), data = _, split = ~group, vcov = "hetero") |>
    coeftable(keep = "pop") |>
    transmute(group = as.character(sample), b = Estimate, se = `Std. Error`)
}

by_occupation <- skill |>
  left_join(premium_by_occupation(health), by = "OCCP") |>
  left_join(concentration_by(OCCP), by = c("OCCP" = "group"),
            suffix = c("", "_conc")) |>
  mutate(top = mean_wage >= top_cutoff)
top_conc <- concentration_by(top)

# Top earners against other healthcare workers, comparing workers in the same
# occupation. The second model's interaction is the gap between the groups.
top_vs_rest <- function(data) {
  groups <- feols(log(wage) ~ i(top, log(pop)) + AGEP + I(AGEP^2) + female | OCCP,
                  data = data, weights = ~PWGTP, cluster = ~cbsa)
  gap <- feols(log(wage) ~ log(pop) + log(pop):top + AGEP + I(AGEP^2) + female | OCCP,
               data = data, weights = ~PWGTP, cluster = ~cbsa)
  tibble(group = c("Other healthcare", "Top earners", "Gap"),
         b = c(coef(groups)[c("top::FALSE:log(pop)", "top::TRUE:log(pop)")],
               coef(gap)[["log(pop):topTRUE"]]),
         se = c(se(groups)[c("top::FALSE:log(pop)", "top::TRUE:log(pop)")],
                se(gap)[["log(pop):topTRUE"]]))
}
main <- top_vs_rest(health)
younger <- top_vs_rest(filter(health, AGEP < 50))
older <- top_vs_rest(filter(health, AGEP >= 50))
lower_cutoff <- top_vs_rest(mutate(health, top = mean_wage >= 150000))

# Precision-weighted lines through the occupation estimates, and the same
# premium line for workers aged 50-64 only
fit_premium <- lm(b ~ log(mean_wage), data = by_occupation, weights = 1 / se^2)
fit_conc <- lm(b_conc ~ log(mean_wage), data = by_occupation, weights = 1 / se_conc^2)
fit_older <- lm(b ~ log(mean_wage), weights = 1 / se^2,
                data = left_join(skill, premium_by_occupation(filter(health, AGEP >= 50)),
                                 by = "OCCP"))
p_value <- function(fit) summary(fit)$coefficients[2, 4]

# For slide text and charts
pct <- function(x) paste0(if_else(x < 0, "−", "+"), abs(round(x)), "%")
interval <- function(row) {
  paste0(pct(big_vs_small(row$b - 1.96 * row$se)), " to ",
         pct(big_vs_small(row$b + 1.96 * row$se)))
}
top_names <- by_occupation |> filter(top) |> arrange(desc(mean_wage)) |> pull(occupation)
next_best <- by_occupation |> filter(!top) |> slice_max(mean_wage)
labelled <- c("Surgeons", "Physicians", "Dentists", "Nurse Anesthetists",
              "Pharmacists", "Registered Nurses", "Physician Assistants",
              "Medical Assistants", "Home Health Aides")
wage_range <- range(by_occupation$mean_wage)
group_colours <- c(`TRUE` = "#c0392b", `FALSE` = "#2a78d6")

# Values beyond a chart's axis limits are drawn at the edge as triangles, so
# a few imprecise estimates do not stretch the chart
squish_to <- function(x, limits) pmin(pmax(x, limits[1]), limits[2])
off_scale_shapes <- c(`FALSE` = 16, `TRUE` = 17)
```

## Thesis

```{r code-thesis, ref.label=c("setup", "download", "data", "models"), eval=FALSE}
```

::: {.key-point}
Big U.S. cities pay most healthcare workers more, but not the best-paid. Top earners give up the big-city premium to live in big cities, as if big-city variety were a luxury they buy.
:::

- **Evidence:** `r scales::comma(nrow(health))` full-time healthcare wage earners in `r nrow(metro_pop)` U.S. metro areas, 2024 American Community Survey.
- **Comparison:** workers in the same occupation, in metros of different sizes.
- **What we add:** Lee (2010) found this pattern in 2000 data. We test it 24 years later.

::: {.notes}
Speaker 1 presents slides 2–5; Speaker 2 presents slides 6–10. About 30 seconds. "Big cities pay more" is common knowledge; the surprise is that the best-paid workers are not paid more there.
:::

## Two explanations, two predictions

| | Productivity spillovers | Consumer city |
|---|---|---|
| Why big cities pay more | Workers are more productive there | Housing costs more; most workers need compensation |
| Pay of top-skill workers in big cities | **Higher**, like everyone else's | **Not higher**: they value variety, a luxury good |

::: {.key-point}
Test where the explanations disagree: the pay of the highest-skill workers.
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. This slide is the heart of the design. Both explanations agree that average wages are higher in big cities, so average wages cannot tell them apart. Only the consumer-city explanation predicts that top-skill workers are not paid more.
:::

## The better an occupation pays, the smaller its big-city premium

```{r code-premium, ref.label=c("setup", "download", "data", "models", "premium-chart"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: premium-chart
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
premium_limits <- c(-15, 22)
premium_points <- by_occupation |>
  mutate(label = if_else(occupation %in% labelled, occupation, NA),
         y = big_vs_small(b),
         off_scale = !between(y, premium_limits[1], premium_limits[2]),
         y = squish_to(y, premium_limits))

ggplot(premium_points, aes(mean_wage, y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("line", x = wage_range,
           y = big_vs_small(predict(fit_premium, tibble(mean_wage = wage_range))),
           colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = top, shape = off_scale), size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 4.5, na.rm = TRUE,
                  min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(),
                breaks = c(50000, 100000, 200000, 400000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = premium_limits, labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = off_scale_shapes, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Average wage of the occupation (log scale)",
       y = "Pay, 5M vs 250k metro") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

Each dot is one of `r nrow(by_occupation)` occupations; red: top earners ($200,000+). Triangles: `r sum(premium_points$off_scale)` beyond the axis, drawn at its edge.

::: footer
Log wage on log metro population, with age and sex, for each occupation; full-time wage earners aged 25–64. Line weighted by precision.
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1.5 minutes. Read the chart left to right: aides and nurses earn more in big cities, as everyone expects. The line falls as occupations pay more, and the top earners (`r paste(top_names, collapse = ", ")`) sit below zero.
:::

## Top earners are paid no more in big cities

```{r code-top, ref.label=c("setup", "download", "data", "models", "top-chart"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: top-chart
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3
main |>
  filter(group != "Gap") |>
  mutate(group = fct_rev(fct_inorder(group))) |>
  ggplot(aes(big_vs_small(b), group, colour = group == "Top earners")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = big_vs_small(b - 1.96 * se),
                      xmax = big_vs_small(b + 1.96 * se)),
                  linewidth = 1.2, size = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Pay in a metro of 5 million vs one of 250,000 (95% interval)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
```

- **Other healthcare workers:** `r pct(big_vs_small(main$b[1]))` in the bigger metro.
- **Top earners** (`r paste(top_names, collapse = ", ")`): `r pct(big_vs_small(main$b[2]))`, with an interval of `r interval(main[2, ])`.

::: footer
Both groups compared with workers in the same occupation; age and sex held fixed. Standard errors clustered by metro.
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. The productivity explanation predicts that top earners gain like everyone else. They do not: relative to other healthcare workers, their big-city pay is `r pct(big_vs_small(main$b[3]))`, with an interval of `r interval(main[3, ])`.
:::

## Yet better-paid occupations concentrate in big cities

```{r code-concentration, ref.label=c("setup", "download", "data", "models", "concentration-chart"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: concentration-chart
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
conc_limits <- c(0.8, 1.25)
conc_points <- by_occupation |>
  mutate(label = if_else(occupation %in% labelled, occupation, NA),
         off_scale = !between(b_conc, conc_limits[1], conc_limits[2]),
         y = squish_to(b_conc, conc_limits))

ggplot(conc_points, aes(mean_wage, y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("line", x = wage_range,
           y = predict(fit_conc, tibble(mean_wage = wage_range)), colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = top, shape = off_scale), size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 4.5, na.rm = TRUE,
                  min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(),
                breaks = c(50000, 100000, 200000, 400000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = conc_limits) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = off_scale_shapes, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Average wage of the occupation (log scale)",
       y = "Concentration in big metros") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

Above 1: more workers per resident in bigger metros. Top earners as a group: `r sprintf("%.2f", top_conc$b[top_conc$group == "TRUE"])`, against `r sprintf("%.2f", top_conc$b[top_conc$group == "FALSE"])` for other healthcare workers. Paid no more, they choose big cities.

::: footer
Poisson regression of each occupation's worker count in every metro on log population. Line weighted by precision. Triangles: beyond the axis.
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. If big-city hospitals could not find top earners at lower pay, they would have fewer of them, not more.
:::

## Alternative: big cities build skills faster?

```{r code-age, ref.label=c("setup", "download", "data", "models"), eval=FALSE}
```

1. **The alternative:** young high-skill workers accept low pay in big cities because their wages grow faster there (Glaeser and Maré 2001).
2. **If it were true:** workers aged 50–64, past most of that growth, would not show the gap.
3. **What we see:** relative to other healthcare workers, top earners' big-city pay is `r pct(big_vs_small(older$b[3]))` for ages 50–64, against `r pct(big_vs_small(younger$b[3]))` for ages 25–49.

::: {.key-point}
The gap is not only about early-career investment.
:::

::: {.notes}
Speaker 2 takes over here. About 1 minute. The 50–64 interval is `r interval(older[3, ])`.
:::

## Where the theory does not apply

```{r code-lawyers, ref.label=c("setup", "download", "data", "models", "lawyers"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: lawyers
#| include: false
lawyers <- feols(log(wage) ~ log(pop) + AGEP + I(AGEP^2) + female,
                 data = filter(workers, OCCP == "2100"),
                 weights = ~PWGTP, cluster = ~cbsa)

# Employed lawyers and physicians per 10,000 residents, small vs large metros
per_resident <- persons |>
  filter(OCCP %in% c("2100", "3090"), ESR %in% 1:2) |>
  inner_join(puma_metro, by = c("STATE", "PUMA")) |>
  count(cbsa, OCCP, wt = PWGTP, name = "workers") |>
  complete(cbsa = metro_pop$cbsa, OCCP, fill = list(workers = 0)) |>
  left_join(metro_pop, by = "cbsa") |>
  mutate(size = case_when(pop < 500000 ~ "small", pop >= 5e6 ~ "large")) |>
  filter(!is.na(size)) |>
  summarise(per_10k = 1e4 * sum(workers) / sum(pop), .by = c(OCCP, size)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = size, values_from = per_10k) |>
  mutate(ratio = small / large)
small_share <- function(code) round(100 * per_resident$ratio[per_resident$OCCP == code])
```

- **Lawyers earn `r round(big_vs_small(coef(lawyers)[["log(pop)"]]))`% more** in a metro of 5 million than in one of 250,000.
- Metros under 500,000 have `r small_share("2100")`% as many lawyers per resident as metros over 5 million, but `r small_share("3090")`% as many physicians.
- Small cities need doctors, not lawyers, so they must pay doctors to come; they need not pay lawyers.

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. Stating where the theory stops is part of the story: it applies to occupations that every city needs.
:::

## What this analysis cannot tell us

```{r code-limits, ref.label=c("setup", "download", "data", "models"), eval=FALSE}
```

- **Mixed evidence by age.** For ages 50–64, the falling line on slide 4 disappears (p = `r round(p_value(fit_older), 2)`, against p = `r signif(p_value(fit_premium), 1)` for all ages); only the top-earner gap holds.
- **Wage earners only.** Self-employed doctors and dentists are left out; their pay may follow a different pattern.
- **One cross-section.** The data compare different workers across cities; following the same workers as they move would need panel data.
- **Non-wage benefits are missing.** Rural loan-repayment programs for doctors are not in wages.

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute.
:::

## Takeaways

- Most healthcare workers earn more in big cities; the best-paid do not, though they choose to live there.
- The pattern Lee (2010) found in 2000 still holds in 2024 for the top earners.
- Small cities pay a premium to attract top professionals, a cost that matters for rural healthcare.

::: {.notes}
About 30 seconds.
:::

## Backup: Sources

- Lee, S. (2010). "Ability sorting and consumer city." *Journal of Urban Economics* 68(1): 20–33.
- Glaeser, E. L., and D. C. Maré (2001). "Cities and skills." *Journal of Labor Economics* 19(2): 316–342.
- Glaeser, E. L., J. Kolko, and A. Saiz (2001). "Consumer city." *Journal of Economic Geography* 1(1): 27–50.
- Data: U.S. Census Bureau, 2024 ACS 1-year PUMS; 2020 tract-to-PUMA relationship file; 2020 metropolitan area delineation.

## Backup: Decision log

1. **Full-time, full-year wage earners aged 25–64,** so that annual wages are comparable.
2. **2020 metro delineation, not 2023.** The 2023 file replaced Connecticut's counties with planning regions, which do not match the 2020 tract file. `r nrow(metro_pop)` of `r n_distinct(metro_counties$cbsa)` metros remain after dropping PUMAs that cross metro boundaries.
3. **At least 200 workers per occupation.** Smaller occupations, such as podiatrists, give unstable estimates. Veterinary occupations are not human healthcare.
4. **Top earners: $200,000 or more.** The next occupation, `r next_best$occupation`, averages `r scales::dollar(next_best$mean_wage, accuracy = 1000)`. With a $150,000 cutoff, top earners' big-city pay is `r pct(big_vs_small(lower_cutoff$b[2]))`.
5. **The data dictionary is not a regular table.** Reading it as one merged the occupation codes and names, so the occupation rows are read separately.
